_readme: ALL game numbers live in this file. Scripts never contain numbers. Every NASA or mission number has a "source": a link to where the real NASA number came from, or a written game-design choice. Layout, look and timing settings (walk, arm, dashboard, ship, power_panel) are game-design choices and have no source. If you add a made-up number for testing, mark its source with the word PLACEHOLDER (in capitals) and replace it with real NASA data, or a written game-design choice that Kaleb passes, before the final submission.

stages._readme: The order of the game screens. go_next() in StageManager.gd walks down this list, one screen at a time. Each name is a scene file in the scenes folder (intro means scenes/intro.tscn). To change the order, change this list. Nothing else needs to change.
stages.source: Game-design choice by Kaleb. It is NOT a NASA number.

setup._readme: Settings for the five setup questions (name, who are you, where, what for, rocket). After you answer, the inner voice reacts and a Next button appears; the player clicks it to go on. name_max_length = the most letters the name box accepts. default_character = who you play as if you press Play on a later screen without answering the questions.
setup.source: Game-design choice. It is NOT a NASA number.

_rules_readme: rule "max" = the total must stay AT or BELOW value. rule "min" = the total must reach AT LEAST value. warning = where the dashboard turns yellow (for max: above warning; for min: below warning). bar_max = the number that fills the dashboard bar all the way.

goal_rules._readme: The 3 goal rules of this mission, shown as a checklist on the mission screen. Each name is one of the limits below, so the numbers (4 Gb/day, 24 months, 0.6 Mb/s) are read from the limits and never copied. The wording is in story.json.
goal_rules.source: Written game-design choice by Kaleb (AGENT_SOURCE.md section 2, 2026-11-10): send home at least 4 Gb/day, keep the spacecraft working 24 months, communications at least 0.6 Mb/s. The numbers come from the limits below.

budget.source: MAVEN's total cost (our mission gets MAVEN's money, less than MRO's $720M). value ("Cost: $671 million over its full life cycle.", MAVEN press kit, Quick Facts, page 4): https://mars.nasa.gov/files/resources/MAVEN_PressKit_Final.pdf; warning and bar_max: game-design choice

mass.source: MRO's dry mass (the rocket and the fuel were sized for it). value ("139 kilograms ... science payload, 892 kilograms ... other dry weight": 139 + 892 = 1,031 kg): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; warning and bar_max: game-design choice

power.source: value: game-design choice (the parts cannot use more power than the solar panels make); warning and bar_max: game-design choice (warning 250 makes every small solar panel build yellow)

communications.source: What MRO could still send when Mars is farthest from Earth. value ("expected to send data to a 34-meter antenna on Earth at a rate of about 600 kilobits per second" = 0.6 Mb/s): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; warning and bar_max: game-design choice

data.source: value: game-design choice (just under the basic camera's 4.8 Gb/day, so the basic camera only passes if it is switched off for a short time at most, about 10 seconds; MRO's planned "26 terabits or more" is all six instruments, not one camera); warning and bar_max: game-design choice

mission_lifetime.source: MRO's primary science phase. value ("a low-altitude orbit around Mars for two years"; "Primary science phase: November 2006 to December 2008"): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; warning and bar_max: game-design choice

characters._readme: The three characters. The character is the ONLY place that says which level the player plays (easy, medium or hard), so the character and the level can never disagree. What each level changes (budget, timing, supplies, hints) is in data/levels.json.
characters.source: Game-design choice by Kaleb (AGENT_SOURCE.md section 2, 2026-11-10): Scientist = easy, Janitor = medium, Student = hard. It is NOT a NASA number.

launch_vehicles._readme: The three rockets the player can pick. cost = what the rocket costs, in million $. The rocket's cost is added to the Build budget total. The MEDIUM rocket's cost is already taken OUT of the spacecraft base (spacecraft_base budget is 490 minus the medium cost), so with the medium rocket the total is the same as before. The small rocket makes the total lower and the large rocket makes it higher. The rocket does NOT change the mission limits ($671M budget, 1,031 kg mass). How many launch moments each rocket has, and how tight they are, is in data/timing.json. default = the rocket used if you press Play on a later screen without picking one. If you change the medium cost, also change the base budget by the same amount, the other way.

spacecraft_base._readme: The spacecraft body (computer, frame, empty fuel tanks, other instruments) that every build has. Its mass is dry mass: no fuel. Its numbers are added to the parts the player picks. Its power does NOT include the heater: the heater is in "reroute_power", because the player can switch it off.
spacecraft_base.source: MRO spacecraft without the swappable parts. budget is 400 = 490 minus the medium rocket's cost of 90 (the rocket's cost is taken OUT of the base, see "launch_vehicles"; the rocket's 90 is PLACEHOLDER). So the total with the medium rocket is still exactly 490, the same as before the rocket question. The 490 comes from: ("Cost: About $720 million total, consisting approximately of $450 million spacecraft development and science instruments; $90 million launch; $180 million mission operations"; minus the game costs of MRO's parts, large solar 70 + high resolution camera 110 + large antenna 50 = 230: 720 - 230 = 490) and mass ("139 kilograms ... science payload, 892 kilograms ... other dry weight" = 1,031 kg dry; minus MRO's solar arrays 96.6, HiRISE 65 and 3 m antenna 20.7: 1,031 - 96.6 - 65 - 20.7 = 848.7; the 3 kg CTX camera stays in the base): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; power: no public source; communications and data: game-design choice (the body sends and collects nothing by itself); mission_lifetime: game-design choice

_look_readme: "look" = how a part is drawn in the 3D walk. Sizes are in meters and are only for the picture, not NASA data. shape: wings = two flat panels on the sides, size [width, thickness, depth]; cylinder = hangs under the body, size [radius, length]; dish = sits on top, size [radius, depth]. model: leave "" to use the simple shape, or put a path like "res://models/large_antenna.glb" to use a real 3D model.

small.name: Small
small.source: Mars Odyssey solar array. mass: https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20030065626/downloads/20030065626.pdf; power: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/odysseyarrival.pdf; budget: no public source; mission_lifetime: game-design choice

medium.name: Medium
medium.source: MAVEN solar arrays. power: https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2015/03/mavenfactsheet_final20130610.pdf; mass: no public source; budget: no public source; mission_lifetime: game-design choice

large.name: Large
large.source: MRO solar arrays, both wings. mass (2 x 48.3 kg): https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/20070029236/downloads/20070029236.pdf; power: https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; budget: no public source; mission_lifetime: game-design choice

basic.name: Basic
basic.source: MRO Context Camera (CTX). mass ("3 kilograms") and power ("7 watts (imaging)"): https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-reconnaissance-orbiter/science-instruments/; data ("approximately 3.5 Tb" in the primary mission: 3,500 Gb / about 730 days = 4.8 Gb/day): https://pds-imaging.jpl.nasa.gov/data/mro/mars_reconnaissance_orbiter/ctx/mrox_0954/document/ctxsis.pdf; budget: no public source

high_res.name: High resolution
high_res.source: MRO HiRISE camera. mass ("65 kilograms") and power ("60 watts"): https://science.nasa.gov/mission/mars-reconnaissance-orbiter/science-instruments/; data ("more than 12 Tb of HiRISE data during the 2-year" primary mission: 12,000 Gb / 730 days = 16.4 Gb/day; science paper by the HiRISE team, McEwen et al. 2007, JGR): https://boris.unibe.ch/25369/1/2005JE002605.pdf; budget: no public source

small.name: Small
small.source: Mars Odyssey 1.3 m high-gain antenna. mass ("Mass (kg) 3.150"; the catalog says "Masses of MGA and HGA are combined", so this is the high-gain antenna plus the small medium-gain antenna on it): https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/ody/ody-m-rss-1-raw-v1/odrs_0299/catalog/inst.cat; communications ("maximum supported data rate of 124.425 kbps" = 0.124 Mb/s): https://discovery.larc.nasa.gov/PDF_FILES/28Mars_Relay_Description.pdf; power: game-design choice, same 172 W amplifier as MRO (power used, electricity in; Odyssey really sends with "a 15 W Solid State Power Amplifier", from the Mars Relay Description link above; 172 W is the MRO figure): https://descanso.jpl.nasa.gov/DPSummary/MRO_092106.pdf; budget: no public source

large.name: Large
large.source: MRO 3 m high-gain antenna. mass (Table 2-1: "HGA prime reflector 19.1" + "Antenna feed assembly 1.6" = 20.7 kg) and power (Table 2-1, X-band TWTA "Spacecraft power input, W" 172; power used, electricity in; its radio power out is 100 W): https://descanso.jpl.nasa.gov/DPSummary/MRO_092106.pdf; communications (same document: "rates as high as 6 Mbps"; NASA's Mars Relay Description gives a maximum of 5.2 Mbps: https://discovery.larc.nasa.gov/PDF_FILES/28Mars_Relay_Description.pdf); budget: no public source

power_low._readme: The live alarm in the 3D walk: a shadow pass. The spacecraft flies into Mars' shadow, where no sunlight reaches the solar panels. It starts after start_after_seconds. The solar part (solar_part) then makes solar_drop_percent less power (100 = none at all), and the batteries give battery_power watts instead. If spare power goes below the limit, the alarm rings and the player has time_to_fix_seconds to turn systems off at the power panel. The alarm is fixed the moment power fits again (spare power back inside the limit). If it stops fitting while the shadow pass is still on, the alarm rings again. The shadow pass ends storm_seconds after it starts: the solar panels get their full power back, and the player can switch systems back on. IMPORTANT: time_to_fix_seconds must be SHORTER than storm_seconds, or a player who does nothing would be saved when the shadow pass ends.
power_low.source: MRO passing through Mars' shadow. solar_drop_percent ("a pair of nickel-hydrogen batteries to fill in when the spacecraft is in the shadow of a planet": in shadow the solar panels make no power): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; storm_seconds: game-design choice (20 s of the 60 s walk is about one third, like the real shadow: "currently for about 40 minutes of every two-hour orbit", 40 of 112 minutes; this one shadow stands for every real shadow, sped up): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=7059; battery_power: game-design choice (MRO's real batteries are bigger: "two nickel-hydrogen rechargeable batteries, each with an energy storage capacity of 50 ampere-hours -- at 32 volts that's 1,600 watts for one hour" and "only about 40 percent of the battery capacity is ever planned to be used": 2 x 1,600 x 0.4 = 1,280 watt-hours over a 40-minute shadow = about 1,900 W, more than any build uses, so the alarm would never ring; 400 W makes every build switch the antenna or the heater off, like the real team that "reduced the draw on them, in part by adjusting heater temperatures before the spacecraft enters shadow"): http://web.archive.org/web/20090827094624/http://mars.jpl.nasa.gov/mro/mission/sc_electrical.html and https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/news.php?feature=7059; start_after_seconds and time_to_fix_seconds: game-design choice

walk._readme: 3D walk settings. reach_distance = how close (in meters) you must stand to a part to press E on it. voice_hold_seconds = after the inner voice says something, warnings wait this long so they don't talk over it. end_read_seconds = when the mission is over, time to read the last line before the debrief. failed_read_seconds = the same, when the power alarm ran out of time. The mission is over when the mission clock reaches the mission length (the mission's mission_lifetime limit, for example 24 months).

ship._readme: The ship interior (graybox: plain boxes, no art). All sizes are in meters. Seen from above, x goes left/right and z goes front/back (the Bridge is at the front, small z). Each room is a box from x[0] to x[1] and z[0] to z[1]. door = the wall that has the doorway into the hallway (north, south, east or west). The hallway is open at both ends: the Bridge and the Comms room close them off. player_start = where you stand when the mission begins; player_facing_degrees = which way you look (180 = toward the hallway). Each room gets one ceiling light, the hallway gets hallway_lights. sign_letter_size = how tall the room-name letters are (meters). marker_glow = how brightly the station markers glow; the marker_light lights up the floor around them.

station_markers._readme: Glowing floor squares for stations we will build later. Each one = [x, z] on the floor, inside that room. The text is in story.json (ship / future_stations).

power_panel._readme: The power panel in the Power room (the Reroute Power mini-game). position = where its bottom middle stands on the floor, in meters (same x/z map as "ship"; here it stands against the Power room's north wall, which is at z = -5). facing_degrees = which way its front faces (0 = toward +z, into the room; -90 = toward -x). size = [width, height, depth] in meters. height_above_floor = the gap under the cabinet. Colors are web color codes.

reroute_power._readme: The Reroute Power mini-game (the switch panel). systems = the switches, top to bottom. camera and antenna are parts: their power comes from the version the player picked. The heater is not a part: every spacecraft has one, and its effects are added to every build (it used to be inside spacecraft_base). off_lifetime_months_per_second = while the heater is OFF, the cold wears out the batteries: the mission loses this many extra months of lifetime every real second (0.2 = 1 month every 5 seconds).

heater.source: All MRO heaters. power (the page says "As much as 300 watts of power are used to run heaters"; 300 W is that figure, not a sum): https://mars.nasa.gov/mro/mission/spacecraft/parts/thermal/; off_lifetime_months_per_second: game-design choice

dashboard._readme: Dashboard colors (web color codes). safe = inside the limit, warning = close to the limit, danger = past the limit. flash_seconds = how fast a row flashes during an alarm.

mission_clock._readme: The live mission in the 3D walk. months_per_second = how fast mission time runs (0.4 = one real minute is 24 mission months). days_per_month turns months into days for the data total (30.4 = 365.25 days / 12). turned_off_parts_stop = what a part stops giving or using when it is turned off (it still has its mass and cost).
mission_clock.source: months_per_second: game-design choice (0.4 makes the 60-second walk equal MRO's real 24-month primary science phase: "a low-altitude orbit around Mars for two years"; "Primary science phase: November 2006 to December 2008"): https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/news/press_kits/mro-launch-Aug05.pdf; days_per_month: calendar math (365.25 days / 12 = 30.4; 24 x 30.4 = 730 days, the same 730 days used for the camera data, so the basic camera collects 4.8 x 730 = about 3,500 Gb, like CTX's real "approximately 3.5 Tb"); turned_off_parts_stop: game rule (a part that is turned off still has its mass and cost)

arm._readme: The wrist light on the player's arm. It shows the worst dashboard color. blink_seconds = how fast it blinks when something is red. raise_seconds = how long Tab takes to raise or lower the arm. panel_gap_pixels = space between the wrist light and the dashboard above it.

textures._readme: Textures made in code (scripts/autoload/Textures.gd). They are GRAY: 1.0 = keep the material's color, 0.5 = half as bright. pixels = image size (must divide evenly by squares_across, and by 2 x thread_pixels). meters = how many meters one copy covers. noise_frequency = size of the random bumps (bigger = smaller bumps). seed = which random bumps (same every run). Looks only, not mission numbers.
